pages.title: What Should I Eat with Crohn's or Colitis? | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: Practical IBD diet guidance: foods many people tolerate in remission vs. during flares, hydration, and when to see a dietitian, education only, not medical advice.
pages.h1: What should I eat with Crohn's or colitis?
pages.intro: There is no single diet for inflammatory bowel disease. Triggers differ by person and disease activity. This guide summarizes patterns many patients discuss with their gastroenterologist or IBD dietitian.

sections.heading: During remission
paragraphs: A balanced pattern with fruits, vegetables, lean protein, and whole grains is a common goal when symptoms are quiet.
Some people reintroduce higher-fiber foods slowly with their team's guidance.

sections.heading: During a flare
paragraphs: Softer, lower-fiber choices, bananas, white rice, applesauce, broths, lean protein, are often easier to tolerate temporarily.
Hydration matters when diarrhea or reduced intake is present.

tips: Keep a simple food and symptom log
Introduce one new food at a time
Ask about vitamin D, iron, and B12 labs

related.label: Best foods during a Crohn's flare (article)

faq.q: Is there one best diet for Crohn's disease?
faq.a: No. Individual triggers and disease activity vary. Work with your IBD team for a plan that fits you.

faq.q: Should I avoid all fiber?
faq.a: Not always. Many people reduce fiber during active symptoms and expand variety in remission, with clinician guidance.

pages.title: Foods to Eat During a Crohn's Flare | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: Gentle food ideas, hydration, and common triggers during an active Crohn's flare. Educational guide, not a substitute for your gastroenterologist.
pages.h1: Foods to eat during a Crohn's flare
pages.intro: When inflammation is active, many people focus on easy-to-digest meals and fluids. These are general patterns, not rules that apply to everyone.

sections.heading: Often easier to tolerate
paragraphs: Soft fruits (bananas, applesauce), refined grains (white rice, plain pasta), broth-based soups, eggs, tofu, and lean poultry or fish are frequent choices in patient education materials.

sections.heading: Hydration
paragraphs: Water, oral rehydration solutions, broth, and herbal teas may help when fluid losses are higher. Limit caffeine and alcohol if they worsen symptoms.

tips: Eat smaller, more frequent meals if large portions trigger discomfort
Avoid known personal triggers even if they are healthy for others

related.label: Full article: best foods during a flare

faq.q: Can diet stop a Crohn's flare?
faq.a: Diet alone does not treat inflammation. Medication and medical care from your IBD team are essential; food choices may reduce irritation while you recover.

pages.title: Ulcerative Colitis Diet & Foods | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: UC nutrition basics: remission vs. flare patterns, hydration, and tracking triggers. Educational guide for ulcerative colitis patients and caregivers.
pages.intro: Ulcerative colitis primarily affects the colon. Nutrition goals often include maintaining weight, correcting deficiencies, and identifying foods that worsen symptoms for you personally.

sections.heading: Remission goals
paragraphs: A varied, nutrient-dense pattern supports long-term health when tolerated.
Some patients work with an IBD dietitian on reintroducing fiber and plant foods.

sections.heading: Active symptoms
paragraphs: Lower-fiber, low-residue patterns are sometimes used short term.
See our guide on UC trigger foods for common items patients monitor.

related.label: Foods that may trigger UC symptoms
What should I eat with IBD?

faq.q: Is ulcerative colitis diet the same as Crohn's?
faq.a: Principles overlap, but location of disease and personal triggers differ. Follow guidance tailored to your diagnosis.

pages.title: Crohn's Disease Diet & Nutrition | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: How nutrition fits into Crohn's disease care: deficiencies, flare vs. remission eating, and tools to spot patterns. Education only.
pages.intro: Crohn's can affect any part of the digestive tract, so nutritional needs vary widely. Tracking intake and symptoms helps you bring clearer data to clinic visits.

sections.heading: Why nutrition matters
paragraphs: Malnutrition, anemia, and vitamin deficiencies are common in IBD.
Diet does not replace medication, but it supports energy, growth (in youth), and recovery.

sections.heading: Using data at appointments
paragraphs: A food and symptom log, or IBDPal export, helps your team see patterns between visits.

pages.title: Low-Residue Diet for IBD | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: When a low-residue or low-fiber pattern may be discussed during IBD flares, example foods, and how long to use it, with your care team's input.
pages.intro: A low-residue pattern limits fiber and tough-to-digest foods for a short period for some patients during active symptoms. It is not meant to be permanent without medical supervision.

sections.heading: Common inclusions
paragraphs: Refined grains, peeled cooked vegetables, tender meats, eggs, and smooth dairy (if lactose is tolerated) appear in many patient handouts.

sections.heading: Transition back
paragraphs: As symptoms improve, teams often help reintroduce fiber gradually to support long-term gut health.

pages.title: Hydration & Fluids for IBD | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: Why dehydration is common in IBD, drink choices during flares, and when to call your care team. Educational hydration guide.
pages.intro: Diarrhea, vomiting, and reduced oral intake increase dehydration risk in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

sections.heading: Practical tips
paragraphs: Sip fluids throughout the day; consider electrolyte drinks when losses are high.
Broths and oral rehydration solutions are common suggestions in patient education.

faq.q: When is dehydration an emergency?
faq.a: Dizziness, very dark urine, rapid heartbeat, or inability to keep fluids down warrant urgent medical contact, not only self-care at home.

sections.heading: Contact your team if

pages.title: First Gastroenterology Appointment With IBD | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: What many patients bring, ask, and expect at a first GI visit for Crohn's or colitis. Educational prep guide, not medical advice.
pages.intro: Your first visit with a gastroenterologist or IBD specialist sets the tone for ongoing care. Arriving with basic records and questions helps you use the time well.

sections.heading: Before the visit
paragraphs: Gather prior test results, imaging reports, and a list of current medications and supplements.
Note symptom patterns: stool frequency, blood, pain location, weight changes, and fatigue.
Write down your top three questions so they do not get lost if the visit runs short.

sections.heading: What to bring
paragraphs: Insurance card, photo ID, and referral paperwork if your plan requires it.
A symptom and food log, or an IBDPal export, if you have been tracking.
Names and contact details for prior doctors or hospitals.

sections.heading: Questions patients often ask
paragraphs: What type of IBD do I have, and where is inflammation located?
What tests are needed next, and when will we review results?
What should I do if symptoms worsen before the follow-up visit?

tips: Ask who to call after hours
Request a visit summary or patient portal access
Bring a family member or friend if you want support taking notes

faq.q: How long does a first GI appointment usually take?
faq.a: Timing varies by clinic. Many first visits run 30 to 60 minutes including intake, exam, and planning next steps.

faq.q: Should I change my diet before the first visit?
faq.a: Do not start major diet changes without guidance unless your referring doctor told you to. A simple symptom log is often more helpful than eliminating many foods at once.

pages.title: IBD Flare Emergency Supplies & Go-Bag | IBDPal Guide
pages.description: Checklist of supplies many patients pack for urgency, school, work, and travel during Crohn's or colitis flares. Education only.
pages.h1: IBD flare emergency supplies and go-bag
pages.intro: A small kit reduces stress when bathroom access is uncertain. Customize contents for age, activity, and what your care team recommends.

sections.heading: Core supplies
paragraphs: Travel wipes, spare underwear, discreet disposal bags, and hand sanitizer.
Panty liners or pads if helpful for your symptoms.
A gentle barrier cream if your clinician suggests it for irritated skin.

sections.heading: Information to carry
paragraphs: Clinician name, clinic phone, and after-hours instructions.
Medication list and any as-needed meds approved for travel or school.
Insurance card for unexpected urgent visits.

sections.heading: School and workplace
paragraphs: Duplicate kits in a nurse's office or desk drawer when accommodations allow.
Know restroom locations on your route; practice accessing supplies quickly and discreetly.

tips: Refresh kits after use
Keep one bag at home and one in your daily carry
Add comfort items: headphones, calming music, or a short note from family

related.label: When to go to the ER

faq.q: Does a go-bag replace medical treatment?
faq.a: No. Supplies help you manage urgency with dignity while you follow your flare plan and contact your IBD team.

pages.title: Dining Out With IBD | Restaurant Guide | IBDPal
pages.description: How many patients plan restaurant meals with Crohn's or colitis: menus, portions, restrooms, and social situations. Individual triggers vary.
pages.intro: Restaurants combine unpredictable ingredients with social pressure. Planning around your known patterns and current disease activity can make meals more enjoyable.

sections.heading: Before you go
paragraphs: Preview menus online when possible.
Choose locations with reliable restroom access.
Eat a small safe snack at home if arriving very hungry leads to rushed choices.

sections.heading: Ordering strategies
paragraphs: Simple preparations (grilled protein, plain rice, broth soups) are common starting points during sensitive weeks.
Ask about hidden dairy, spice levels, and high-fiber sides.
Smaller portions or to-go boxes reduce pressure to finish large plates.

sections.heading: After the meal
paragraphs: Log what you ate and how you felt; patterns build a personal shortlist over time.
If symptoms flare, contact your team using your usual flare plan.

tips: Use brief scripts if you want to decline food without a long explanation
Pack approved medications or supplies
Track meals in IBDPal or a notebook

faq.q: Are there safe restaurant foods for everyone with IBD?
faq.a: No single menu works for all patients. Triggers and tolerance change with disease activity. Work with your IBD team on choices that fit you.

pages.title: Camp Oasis & Youth IBD Support | Crohn's & Colitis Foundation | IBDPal
pages.description: How Camp Oasis and Foundation youth resources support kids and teens with Crohn's or colitis. Attribution to the Crohn's & Colitis Foundation. Education only.
pages.h1: Camp Oasis and youth IBD support
pages.intro: Selected Crohn's & Colitis Foundation educational content and Marks are used on IBDPal under license. Camp Oasis is a Foundation program for children and teens with IBD. Confirm current sessions, eligibility, and medical requirements on the Foundation website. IBDPal does not run Camp Oasis and is not endorsed by the Foundation.

sections.heading: What Camp Oasis is
paragraphs: Camp Oasis is the Foundation's summer program for youth living with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
Sessions are designed so medication routines, dietary needs, and bathroom access are part of normal camp life, with medical volunteers on site.
Many families describe camp as the first place their child meets other kids who understand IBD.

sections.heading: Who it is for
paragraphs: The Foundation typically serves children entering grades 2 through 12, with cabin groups by age.
There may be in-person regional camps and virtual options such as CampOasis@Home. Availability changes by year and location.
Always verify age ranges, health forms, and registration deadlines on the Foundation Camp Oasis pages.

sections.heading: How to use Foundation youth education
paragraphs: Beyond camp, the Foundation publishes kids, parents, and teens education for school, friendships, and talking about IBD at home.
Use Foundation pages as the original source, then bring questions to your pediatric GI or IBD team.
IBDPal can help families track symptoms, meals, and school notes between visits.

tips: Start registration early; popular sessions fill up
Ask your GI team about medical forms and medication plans for camp
Pair Foundation youth pages with school accommodation planning

faq.q: Does IBDPal operate Camp Oasis?
faq.a: No. Camp Oasis is a Crohn's & Colitis Foundation program. IBDPal links to Foundation pages under license for education and does not claim partnership or endorsement.

faq.q: Is Camp Oasis medical treatment?
faq.a: No. Camp offers supported recreation and peer connection. Medication and disease decisions stay with your child's IBD care team.

pages.title: IBD Prior Authorization Help | Crohn's & Colitis Foundation Guide | IBDPal
pages.description: How patients use Crohn's & Colitis Foundation prior authorization education with clinic support. Attribution to the Foundation. Not insurance or medical advice.
pages.intro: Selected Crohn's & Colitis Foundation educational content and Marks are used on IBDPal under license. Many IBD therapies require prior authorization. The Foundation publishes patient guidance on navigating approvals, denials, and appeals. Your clinic and insurer decide your case. The Foundation does not endorse IBDPal.

sections.heading: Why prior authorization happens
paragraphs: Insurers often require paperwork before covering specialty IBD medications, infusions, or certain tests.
Step therapy rules may ask you to try another drug first. That can delay care if it does not match your clinician's plan.
Foundation advocacy materials explain common patient rights and appeal pathways in plain language.

sections.heading: How to use Foundation materials
paragraphs: Read the Foundation prior authorization guide on the Foundation website as the original source.
Share denial letters and appeal letter templates with your clinic's prior auth or infusion coordinator.
Track refill dates, infusion schedules, and portal messages so gaps are visible early.

sections.heading: What IBDPal can help with
paragraphs: IBDPal helps you log symptoms and medications so your team has clearer visit notes while insurance reviews continue.
We do not submit prior authorizations or negotiate with insurers on your behalf.

tips: Save denial letters and case numbers
Ask who at the clinic owns prior auth follow-up
Note refill and infusion dates in a calendar or IBDPal

faq.q: Can Foundation materials guarantee approval?
faq.a: No. They educate patients and caregivers. Coverage decisions belong to your insurer and your clinical documentation.

faq.q: Should I stop medication while waiting?
faq.a: Do not stop prescribed therapy without instructions from your IBD clinician. Ask the clinic what to do if a refill or infusion is delayed.

pages.title: Foundation Diet & Nutrition Resources | Crohn's & Colitis | IBDPal
pages.description: How to use Crohn's & Colitis Foundation diet and nutrition education with IBDPal tracking. Attribution to the Foundation. Education only, not a meal plan.
pages.intro: Selected Crohn's & Colitis Foundation educational content and Marks are used on IBDPal under license. Foundation patient education covers diet patterns, working with an IBD dietitian, and nutrition during flares and remission. Use Foundation pages as the original source. Individual plans belong with your clinician. The Foundation does not endorse IBDPal.

sections.heading: What Foundation nutrition education covers
paragraphs: Patient materials often explain that there is no single IBD diet, and that needs change with disease activity, surgery history, and age.
Topics commonly include flare-friendly textures, nutrient gaps, and when to involve a registered dietitian experienced in IBD.
Always confirm details on current Foundation pages, because recommendations and program links can update.

sections.heading: How IBDPal fits beside Foundation education
paragraphs: Read Foundation nutrition education first for trusted patient framing.
Use IBDPal or another log to capture meals, symptoms, and hydration so your GI or dietitian can review real patterns.
Bring questions from Foundation reading to your next visit instead of making major diet changes alone.

sections.heading: Safety boundaries
paragraphs: Diet does not replace medication for inflammation.
Exclusive enteral nutrition and other therapeutic diets should only start under clinical supervision.
Seek urgent care guidance for dehydration, inability to keep fluids down, or rapid weight loss.

tips: Note tolerated foods during quiet weeks vs flare weeks
Ask about vitamin D, iron, B12, and protein goals
Pair Foundation reading with an IBD dietitian referral when possible

pages.title: Anti-Inflammatory Diet for IBD | Realistic Guide | IBDPal
pages.description: What anti-inflammatory eating means for Crohn's and colitis: Mediterranean-style patterns, marketing claims vs evidence, and when to see a dietitian. Education only.
pages.h1: Anti-inflammatory diet for IBD: a realistic guide
pages.intro: Anti-inflammatory diet is a popular search phrase. For IBD, the useful idea is usually a Mediterranean-style pattern rich in plants, olive oil, fish, and fiber when tolerated, not a miracle cleanse. Diet supports care; it does not replace medication for inflammation.

sections.heading: What the phrase usually means
paragraphs: Many clinicians discuss Mediterranean-style eating: vegetables, fruits, legumes when tolerated, whole grains in remission, olive oil, nuts if tolerated, and fish.
Marketing detox teas and extreme elimination kits are not the same as evidence-informed nutrition therapy.

sections.heading: Flare vs remission
paragraphs: During active symptoms, softer textures and temporary fiber reductions may be easier. In quieter weeks, variety and nutrient density matter more.
Track personal triggers instead of copying someone else's forever-ban list.

sections.heading: How to use IBDPal beside diet advice
paragraphs: Log meals and symptoms for two to four weeks before major changes.
Bring the log to your gastroenterologist or IBD dietitian.

tips: Prefer food patterns over supplement stacks sold as anti-inflammatory cures
Ask about vitamin D, iron, and protein needs
Reintroduce foods with a plan, not fear alone

related.label: What should I eat with Crohn's or colitis?

faq.q: Can an anti-inflammatory diet put Crohn's in remission alone?
faq.a: No. Nutrition can support comfort and nutrient status. Inflammatory control usually requires medical therapy guided by your IBD team.

faq.q: Is Mediterranean eating safe in a flare?
faq.a: Parts of it may need texture changes during active symptoms. Ask your clinician or dietitian how to adapt the pattern for you.

pages.title: Iron Deficiency Nutrition in IBD | Food and Clinic Guide
pages.description: Iron-rich eating with Crohn's or colitis, why oral iron may fail during inflammation, and questions for IV vs oral therapy. Education only.
pages.intro: Iron deficiency and anemia are common in IBD because of blood loss, inflammation, and absorption limits. Food helps, but labs and therapy decisions belong with your care team.

sections.heading: Food patterns that support iron
paragraphs: Lean meats, poultry, fish, eggs, legumes if tolerated, and iron-fortified foods are common building blocks.
Vitamin C-containing foods with plant iron sources may help absorption for some people.

sections.heading: Why food is not always enough
paragraphs: Active inflammation can lock iron away. Small-bowel disease or surgery can limit absorption. Oral iron may worsen stools for some patients.
IV iron is sometimes appropriate; that is a clinical decision.

sections.heading: Track and report
paragraphs: Note fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, and stool blood.
Bring hemoglobin and ferritin questions to clinic rather than guessing supplement doses.

tips: Do not start high-dose iron without clinician advice
Pair reading with anemia article and visit prep
Ask whether oral or IV iron fits your disease activity

faq.q: Which iron-rich foods are gentlest in a flare?
faq.a: Tolerance varies. Soft proteins and fortified foods are often easier than high-fiber plant sources during active symptoms. Ask your dietitian.

faq.q: Can I fix IBD anemia with spinach alone?
faq.a: Usually not when bleeding or inflammation is ongoing. Food supports recovery; treating IBD activity and using prescribed iron therapy matter more.

pages.title: Vitamin D and Bone Nutrition in IBD | Patient Guide
pages.description: Vitamin D, calcium, and bone-friendly nutrition for Crohn's and colitis, plus screening questions after steroids. Education only.
pages.h1: Vitamin D and bone nutrition in IBD
pages.intro: Low vitamin D is common in IBD. Bone health also depends on calcium intake, weight-bearing activity when safe, inflammation control, and steroid history.

sections.heading: Why vitamin D matters
paragraphs: Vitamin D supports bone mineralization and is often repleted when labs are low.
Sunlight, fortified foods, and supplements may all play roles; dosing should follow labs and clinician advice.

sections.heading: Calcium food sources
paragraphs: Dairy if tolerated, fortified alternatives, canned fish with bones, and tofu set with calcium are frequent options.
If dairy triggers symptoms, plan alternatives with a dietitian rather than dropping calcium entirely.

sections.heading: Steroids and screening
paragraphs: Repeated systemic steroids raise bone-loss risk.
Ask about DEXA timing and steroid-sparing plans.

tips: Recheck vitamin D rather than guessing high doses
Pair with bone health article
Mention fracture history and menopause status at visits

faq.q: What vitamin D level should I target?
faq.a: Targets vary by lab and clinician. Ask for your number and the plan to recheck after repletion.

faq.q: Do I need calcium pills if I eat dairy?
faq.a: Not always. Total intake from food and supplements matters. Your team personalizes this, especially with kidney stone history.

pages.title: Protein Intake During an IBD Flare | Healing Guide
pages.description: Why protein matters during Crohn's or colitis flares, gentler protein ideas, and when to ask about oral nutrition supplements. Education only.
pages.h1: Protein for healing during an IBD flare
pages.intro: Inflammation and poor intake can speed muscle and nutrient loss. Soft, tolerated proteins help many people meet needs while medications calm disease. This is supportive nutrition, not a cure.

sections.heading: Why protein rises in importance
paragraphs: Tissue repair, immune function, and preventing excess muscle loss all need adequate protein.
Needs may be higher during active disease; your clinician or dietitian sets targets.

sections.heading: Often easier options
paragraphs: Eggs, yogurt if tolerated, tofu, fish, ground poultry, smoothies with protein powder approved by your team, and oral nutrition drinks when food volume is low.
Large steaks and high-fiber beans may be harder mid-flare.

sections.heading: When to escalate
paragraphs: Rapid weight loss, inability to keep food down, or known strictures need prompt clinical contact.
Exclusive enteral nutrition is a supervised therapy, not a DIY protocol.

tips: Spread protein across smaller meals
Log intake for clinic
Ask before starting unfamiliar supplements

faq.q: How many grams of protein do I need in a flare?
faq.a: It depends on weight, disease activity, and kidney function. Ask your IBD dietitian for a personal range.

faq.q: Are protein shakes safe with IBD?
faq.a: Some are well tolerated; others contain sugar alcohols or fibers that worsen symptoms. Check labels with your clinician.

pages.title: Elimination Diets in IBD: When to Stop and Reintroduce
pages.description: How long IBD elimination trials should last, malnutrition risks, reintroduction steps, and dietitian roles. Education only, not a protocol.
pages.h1: Elimination diets in IBD: when to stop
pages.intro: Short, supervised elimination trials can identify triggers. Open-ended restriction without reintroduction raises malnutrition and fear-of-food risk. Know when to stop narrowing and start rebuilding.

sections.heading: A safer mental model
paragraphs: Define the question (for example, dairy or a FODMAP group), the time box, and the reintroduction plan before you start.
Celiac screening should happen before long gluten-free trials.

sections.heading: Red flags to stop the trial early
paragraphs: Unintentional weight loss, fear of almost all foods, nutrient gaps, or worsening pain and obstruction symptoms.
Call your team rather than cutting more food groups alone.

sections.heading: Reintroduction
paragraphs: Add one item at a time, log symptoms for a few days, and keep foods that stay quiet.
Work with an IBD dietitian for structured plans such as guided FODMAP work.

tips: Time-box trials in weeks, not forever
Protect protein and calorie intake while testing
Use IBDPal logs so reintroduction has data

faq.q: How long should an IBD elimination diet last?
faq.a: Many supervised trials are measured in weeks with a planned end. Forever diets without review increase nutrition risk.

faq.q: Should I eliminate five food groups at once?
faq.a: Usually no. Broad cuts make it harder to learn what mattered and easier to lose weight. Ask for a structured plan.

pages.title: Autoimmune Nutrition Basics | Realistic Starter Guide | IBDPal
pages.description: Autoimmune nutrition basics: protect protein and calories, correct deficiencies, avoid extreme marketing diets. Education for broader autoimmune audiences.
pages.intro: Nutrition supports energy and nutrient status in many autoimmune conditions. It does not replace disease-modifying therapy. Use this as a starter map, then personalize with your clinician or dietitian.

sections.heading: Priorities that travel across diagnoses
paragraphs: Meet calorie and protein needs during flares or poor appetite.
Check and replete iron, B12, vitamin D, and other labs when ordered.
Prefer food patterns over detox products.

sections.heading: When elimination is reasonable
paragraphs: Time-boxed trials with a reintroduction plan are safer than forever restriction.
Celiac disease requires a strict gluten-free diet after proper testing.

sections.heading: If you also have IBD
paragraphs: Use IBD-specific flare textures and Foundation or AGA nutrition education alongside this overview.
Log meals and symptoms so GI and dietitian visits have data.

tips: Ask before starting specialty supplements on immunosuppression
Reintroduce foods on purpose
Pair with research publications for evidence context

faq.q: Is there one autoimmune diet?
faq.a: No. Needs differ by diagnosis, medications, surgeries, and tolerances. Marketing lists oversimplify.

faq.q: Can diet put autoimmune disease in remission alone?
faq.a: Diet can support comfort and nutrition. Disease control usually requires medical therapy guided by specialists.

pages.title: Gluten-Free for Autoimmune Conditions: When It Applies
pages.description: When gluten-free eating is medically required versus optional in autoimmune life. Screening-first guidance. Education only.
pages.h1: Gluten-free eating for autoimmune conditions: when it applies
pages.intro: Gluten-free diets are required for celiac disease. For other autoimmune diagnoses, evidence is mixed and unrestricted gluten avoidance can create nutrient gaps. Screen before long trials.

sections.heading: Required vs optional
paragraphs: Celiac disease: strict gluten-free diet after confirmed diagnosis.
Non-celiac autoimmune conditions: gluten-free is not automatically evidence-based treatment.

sections.heading: Screen first
paragraphs: Ask about celiac testing while still eating gluten.
If tests are negative, any trial should be time-boxed with reintroduction.

sections.heading: IBD overlap
paragraphs: People with IBD have higher celiac rates than the general population, so screening questions still matter.

tips: Do not start lifelong gluten-free eating before testing if celiac is possible
Watch fiber, iron, and B vitamins on packaged gluten-free foods
Work with a dietitian for balanced swaps

faq.q: Should everyone with autoimmune disease go gluten-free?
faq.a: No. Celiac disease requires it. Other conditions need individualized advice after proper evaluation.

faq.q: Can I test for celiac after months gluten-free?
faq.a: Testing is often less reliable after prolonged gluten avoidance. Ask your clinician how to proceed.
